title: Speech Acts & Politeness Theory

pts: An utterance can perform an act — requesting, promising, apologising — beyond simply stating a fact.
The same speech act can be performed with wildly different grammatical forms, and the same form can perform different acts in different contexts.
This reframes 'teaching requests' as teaching a function, not a fixed grammatical structure.
points.who: J.L. Austin's Speech Act Theory; John Searle's development of it

items: Give groups twelve cards, each with an utterance.
Groups sort the cards by what they do (request, apology, offer, complaint), not by their grammar.
Discuss cards that could belong to more than one group, depending on context.
Learners order the request cards from most to least direct.
Each learner writes two more ways to make the same request.
Use utterances collected from school notices, WhatsApp messages and shop signs.
Support: provide the function headings with one example each.
Challenge: learners describe a context in which one card would perform a different act.

lines: Open the window. / Could you open the window? / Would you mind opening the window? / It’s very hot in here. / I was wondering if we could get some air.
S1: ‘It’s very hot in here’ is not a request. It’s a statement.
S2: But if the teacher says it and looks at the window, it is a request.

blocks.x: The same act can take many forms, and the same form can perform different acts (Austin 1962; Searle 1969). A syllabus item called ‘requests’ is therefore a function, not a single structure.

body: Purpose: to show one function realized by many forms. Content: a room labelled ‘Request’ with five doors, each labelled with a different utterance, from blunt to indirect. Style: simple architectural drawing. Board version: a box with five arrows pointing into it.

items: Wordwall (free basic plan, limited activities) for a sorting game.

blocks.x: Cards cut from used paper and sorted on the bench.

pts: 'Can you close the window?' is grammatically a question but pragmatically a request — an indirect speech act.
Learners who process only the literal grammatical meaning miss the pragmatic force entirely.
Explicit teaching of common indirect speech act patterns closes a real, persistent comprehension gap.

v: A list of indirect utterances; a short audio or teacher-read dialogue

items: Read aloud eight utterances that look like questions or statements.
Learners decide quickly whether each is really a question, a request, an invitation or a complaint.
Learners give the most natural response to each.
Pairs write and perform a short scene containing three indirect speech acts.
Watch a short scene from an English-language film and note every indirect request.
Support: give a choice of two responses for each utterance.
Challenge: learners write literal responses to show the humour of misreading.

lines: T: Do you know what time it is?
S1: Yes.
T: (waits)
S2: It’s ten past eleven, ma’am.
T: Right. Why did S1’s answer sound strange?
S3: Because you didn’t want to know if he knows. You wanted the time.

blocks.x: Searle (1975) called these indirect speech acts. Learners who process only literal meaning miss their force, so explicit attention to common patterns such as Can you…?, Do you mind…? and Why don’t you…? is worthwhile.

body: Figure 53.2 What the words say, what the speaker does

Purpose: to show the two layers of an indirect speech act. Content: a speech bubble reading ‘Can you close the door?’ with two labels beneath: ‘form: question about ability’ and ‘force: request’. Style: clear, two tones. Board version: one bubble with two arrows.

items: YouTube (free, with advertisements) for short clips; check licensing before classroom use.

blocks.x: The teacher reads the utterances aloud with natural intonation.

pts: Brown & Levinson's politeness theory frames communication as managing both speakers' 'face' — their public self-image.
Positive face involves the desire to be liked and approved of; negative face involves the desire not to be imposed upon.
Politeness strategies are choices about how much face-threat a given speech act carries and how to mitigate it.
points.who: Penelope Brown & Stephen Levinson's Politeness Theory

items: Introduce face, and the three factors: power, distance and imposition.
Groups rate each situation from 1 to 3 on each factor.
Groups add the scores and predict how much softening each request needs.
Groups write the request for two contrasting situations.
Compare with the equivalent requests in a home language, noting pronoun and verb choices that show respect.
Use apologies instead of requests, rating the size of the offence.
Support: provide phrase banks for low, medium and high softening.
Challenge: learners find a situation where the scores predict wrongly.

lines: A: Asking your younger brother to lend you his cycle for ten minutes. (power low, distance low, imposition low)
B: Asking the college principal to extend a fee deadline by a month. (power high, distance high, imposition high)
A: Lend me your cycle for a bit, na?
B: I’m sorry to trouble you, sir, but I wanted to ask whether it might be possible to extend my fee deadline by a month. My family’s harvest payment has been delayed.
S1: In Kannada I would say ‘neevu’ to the principal, never ‘neenu’. In English we must use more words to show the same respect.

body: Purpose: to show the three factors in politeness choices. Content: three dials labelled ‘power’, ‘distance’ and ‘imposition’, feeding into a gauge labelled ‘how much softening’. Style: clean control-panel design. Board version: three circles with arrows pointing to a bar.

items: Google Forms (free) to collect groups’ ratings and compare them.

blocks.x: Situation cards and a rating grid on the board.

pts: Hedges ('sort of,' 'I was wondering if') reduce the face-threat of a request, disagreement, or criticism.
Advanced learners often either under-hedge (sounding blunt) or over-hedge (sounding evasive) relative to native norms.
Explicit teaching of hedging density, calibrated to genre and relationship, addresses both failure modes.

v: Three versions of an email disagreeing with a colleague

items: Learners read three versions of the same email: under-hedged, well-hedged and over-hedged.
They underline every hedge and softener.
Groups place each version on a scale from ‘blunt’ to ‘evasive’.
Discuss the effect of each version on the reader.
Learners rewrite the blunt and the evasive versions to reach the middle.
Compare hedging in an academic abstract with hedging in an email to a friend.
Support: provide a list of hedging devices grouped by type (modal verbs, adverbs, introductory phrases).
Challenge: learners explain how much hedging suits a research report and why.

lines: Under-hedged: Your plan is wrong. The budget is too low. Change it.
Well-hedged: I think there may be a problem with the budget. It looks a little low for the number of schools. Could we look at it again?
Over-hedged: I was just perhaps wondering whether it might possibly be the case that the budget could maybe be slightly on the low side, if that’s all right?
S1: The third one is so polite that I don’t know what he wants.

blocks.x: Hedging is central to academic writing, where it signals caution about claims (Hyland 1998), and to workplace talk, where it protects relationships. Advanced learners tend to err in both directions.

body: Figure 53.4 Too hard, too soft, just right

Purpose: to show calibrated hedging. Content: a horizontal scale from ‘blunt’ to ‘evasive’, with three email icons placed along it and the middle zone shaded. Style: clean, with three colours. Board version: a line with three marks and a shaded middle.

items: Google Docs (free) comments for marking hedges.

blocks.x: Three versions on the board; learners come up and underline hedges.

body: When learners over-hedge, the problem is often stacking: several softeners in one sentence. One well-chosen hedge, such as I wonder if… or It seems that…, is usually enough.

pts: Conversational implicature lets a speaker communicate more than their literal words state, relying on shared inference.
Grice's cooperative principle and its maxims (quantity, quality, relevance, manner) explain how listeners generate these inferences.
Misreading implicature is a common, often invisible source of intercultural miscommunication.
points.who: Paul Grice's Cooperative Principle and conversational implicature

items: Introduce Grice’s four maxims in simple terms: say enough, say what is true, be relevant, be clear.
Groups read six dialogues in which one reply seems to break a maxim.
For each, they name the maxim and write the implied meaning.
Pairs write one dialogue of their own with an implicature for others to interpret.
Use examples from advertising slogans or newspaper headlines.
Support: provide the maxim for each dialogue; learners write only the meaning.
Challenge: learners discuss whether the maxims apply equally in their home language.

lines: A: How was Arjun’s presentation?
B: Well, his slides were very colourful.
Maxim: relation or quantity. Implied: The content was weak.
A: Can I borrow your notes for the exam?
B: I have a lot of studying to do tonight.
Maxim: relation. Implied: No.

blocks.x: A reference letter that says only The candidate was always punctual and neatly dressed implies, by what it leaves out, that there is nothing better to say (Grice 1975).

body: Purpose: to summarize the cooperative principle. Content: four signposts labelled ‘Enough’, ‘True’, ‘Relevant’ and ‘Clear’; a speaker steps off the path and a listener’s thought bubble shows the implied meaning. Style: friendly illustration. Board version: four words in a row with a curved arrow.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for pairs to post their dialogues.

blocks.x: Dialogues read aloud by pairs; the class guesses.

pts: Pragmatic norms — how much hedging, how direct a refusal, how a compliment is received — vary significantly across cultures.
This connects directly to Unit 24's intercultural competence, at the level of concrete, teachable pragmatic behaviour.
Pragmatic failure is often misread as rudeness or incompetence rather than a cross-linguistic difference.

items: Groups read four short incidents in which a conversation went wrong between speakers from different backgrounds.
Groups explain what each speaker probably intended and how it was received.
Discuss whether the problem was grammar, vocabulary or pragmatics.
Groups suggest what each speaker could have said, and what the listener could have assumed instead.
Learners write a short incident from their own experience.
Use incidents from call centres or hospitals.
Support: provide a set of possible explanations for each incident.
Challenge: learners analyse an incident using the terms face, hedging and implicature.

lines: Priya, working with a team in another country, emailed: ‘Kindly send the revised file by today evening. Do the needful.’ A colleague replied coldly. Later Priya learned that the phrase had sounded to him like an order.
S1: In India ‘kindly’ is polite. It is what we learn in school.
S2: But maybe for him it sounded formal, like a command from a boss.

blocks.x: Thomas (1983) called this pragmatic failure and noted that it is often misread as rudeness. The point for learners is not that one convention is wrong but that listeners from different backgrounds may read it differently (Unit 24).

body: Purpose: to show pragmatic misunderstanding. Content: two people at laptops; the words of an email travel along a wire that tangles midway, arriving with a different tone. Style: light, sympathetic. Board version: two stick figures with a tangled line between them.

items: Google Docs (free) for a class collection of incidents.

blocks.x: Incidents on slips of paper passed between groups.

pts: Present authentic examples of a speech act across several registers, then have learners categorise the politeness strategies used.
Role-play (Unit 38) is a natural vehicle for practising speech acts under realistic social pressure.
This is one of the highest-value additions a C1-level course can make, given how often it's left implicit elsewhere.

v: Transcripts of an apology in three registers; role cards

items: Learners read three short apologies: to a friend, to a teacher and to a customer.
Groups categorize the strategies used: expressing regret, taking responsibility, explaining, offering repair, promising.
Compare which strategies appear in each register and how they are softened or strengthened.
In the next lesson, pairs role-play apology situations from role cards, with an observer noting strategies.
Pairs repeat the role-play after feedback, using one new strategy.
Follow the same sequence for refusals, which learners often find hardest.
Support: provide a strategy checklist with example phrases.
Challenge: add a complication, such as an angry customer who rejects the first apology.

blocks.x: A customer-service apology (written for this book):

lines: I’m very sorry about the delay with your order. That’s our mistake: the parcel went to the wrong depot. I’ve arranged for it to be delivered tomorrow morning, and we’ve refunded the delivery charge. It won’t happen again.
Ss: Regret, responsibility, explanation, repair, promise.

blocks.x: This sequence moves from awareness to practice, as recommended in teaching guides on pragmatics (Ishihara and Cohen 2010), and uses role-play (Unit 38) to add realistic social pressure.

body: Purpose: to show apology strategies. Content: a speech bubble divided into five coloured segments, each labelled with a strategy. Style: clear, diagrammatic. Board version: a bubble with five labelled lines.

items: A phone’s voice recorder (free) to record role-plays for review.

blocks.x: Role cards and an observer checklist on paper.

pts: Pragmatic competence is difficult to assess reliably, since 'appropriate' varies by context and relationship.
Rubrics should describe context-appropriate ranges of behaviour, not a single correct answer.
This connects to Unit 46's rubric design, extended into pragmatics' genuinely harder assessment territory.

v: Three short task situations; sample learner responses

items: Write three short situations requiring a speech act, such as refusing an invitation from a senior colleague.
Collect or write six responses to each, ranging from inappropriate to appropriate.
With colleagues, sort the responses into three bands and note the reasons.
Write band descriptors that describe a range of acceptable behaviour, not one correct answer.
Trial the rubric on a new set of responses and discuss disagreements.
Use the rubric for peer assessment of role-plays (Unit 43).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Band descriptors for a refusal (written for this book):

lines: 3: Refuses clearly, softens appropriately for the relationship, gives a reason and maintains the relationship (for example, thanks or an alternative).
2: Refuses clearly but softens too much or too little for the relationship; some attention to the relationship.
1: Refusal is unclear or abrupt; the relationship is not attended to.

blocks.x: Because appropriacy depends on context, rubrics for pragmatics should describe ranges of suitable choices. This extends the rubric design of Unit 46 into harder territory.

body: Purpose: to show that appropriate responses fall within a zone. Content: a target with a broad central ring labelled ‘appropriate range’ rather than a single bull’s-eye; several response cards land inside it. Style: clean. Board version: a circle with a wide shaded ring.

items: Google Sheets (free) to compare teachers’ band decisions.

blocks.x: A paper grid for recording band decisions.

body: Choose one speech act your learners need, such as refusing or disagreeing. Teach the awareness-to-role-play sequence from point 7, then assess one role-play with the rubric from point 8. Note which strategies learners added between the first and second attempts.

dek: Unit 53 of 100: the pragmatic machinery beneath every request, apology, and compliment — and why advanced learners still misfire on it despite excellent grammar.

aims.x: A learner who writes I want two days’ leave. Grant it. has made no grammatical error, yet the message may damage a working relationship. This unit examines the pragmatic machinery beneath requests, apologies, refusals and compliments: what utterances do, how listeners infer what is meant, and how speakers protect each other’s self-image. It extends the previews of pragmatics in Units 24 and 27 into a framework that teachers can analyse, teach and assess.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain speech act theory and teach requests and apologies as functions rather than fixed structures;
help learners recognize the force of indirect speech acts;
use the concepts of face, power, distance and imposition to analyse politeness choices;
teach hedging and mitigation calibrated to genre and relationship;
explain Grice’s cooperative principle and use it to interpret implicature;
treat cross-cultural pragmatic failure as a difference to explore, not a fault to punish;
design an explicit speech-act teaching sequence ending in role-play;
assess pragmatic competence with rubrics that describe appropriate ranges.

why: Why this matters. Pragmatic failure is often invisible to the speaker but not to the listener — a grammatically perfect utterance can still land as rude, cold, or confusing.

background.x: The philosopher J. L. Austin (1962) observed that many utterances are not statements that can be true or false but actions: to say I promise or I apologize is to promise or apologize. John Searle (1969) developed this into a theory of speech acts, and later (1975) explained indirect speech acts, in which one act is performed by means of another, as when Can you pass the salt? functions as a request. Paul Grice (1975) proposed that conversation rests on a cooperative principle with four maxims, of quantity, quality, relation and manner. When a speaker appears to break a maxim, listeners infer an additional meaning, which Grice called an implicature.

Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson (1987) placed these ideas within a theory of politeness built on the concept of face, a person’s public self-image. Positive face is the wish to be liked and approved of; negative face is the wish not to be imposed upon. Requests, criticisms and refusals threaten face, and speakers soften them to a degree that depends on the power difference between the speakers, the social distance between them and the size of the imposition. Their claim to universality has been debated, but the framework remains a practical tool. Comparative studies of requests and apologies across languages have shown both shared strategies and real differences in directness (Blum-Kulka, House and Kasper 1989).

Pragmatic development does not automatically follow grammatical development. Kathleen Bardovi-Harlig and Zoltán Dörnyei (1998) found that EFL learners and their teachers tended to judge grammatical errors as more serious than pragmatic ones, while learners living in an English-speaking environment showed the reverse pattern. Jenny Thomas (1983) warned that pragmatic failure is often judged more harshly than grammatical error, because listeners attribute it to the speaker’s character rather than to their English.

For Indian learners the picture is rich. Kannada, Hindi, Tamil and Urdu encode respect grammatically, for example through choice of second-person pronoun (neevu/neenu, aap/tum), and many learners are highly skilled at managing politeness in these languages. Indian English has its own well-established pragmatic conventions, such as kindly in requests. The aim is not to replace these with British or American norms but to widen learners’ repertoire so that they can choose appropriately for each audience (Unit 74).

items: Speech-act sorting. Learners classify utterances by function and explain one that depends on context.
Politeness analysis. Learners analyse a request using power, distance and imposition and write a suitable version.
Role-play performance. An apology or refusal role-play scored with a range-based rubric.
Critical incident. A written analysis of a personal or given incident, naming the pragmatic concepts involved.
When did a learner’s English last sound rude to you although the grammar was correct? What was happening?
How do your learners manage politeness in their home languages? How could you build on that?
Does your syllabus teach requests as functions or as structures?
Do your learners over-hedge, under-hedge, or both?
How do you respond to Indian English pragmatic conventions such as kindly or do the needful?
How could you assess appropriacy fairly?

terms.def: The suitability of a word, phrase or style for its context, purpose and audience; a sentence can be grammatically correct but inappropriate, such as an overly direct request to a principal.
Meaning that a speaker implies rather than states, which the listener infers from context (Grice 1975); for example, ‘It is cold in here’ may be a request to close the window.

Grice’s (1975) principle that speakers normally cooperate by making their contributions informative, truthful, relevant and clear; implied meanings often arise when a speaker appears to break one of these maxims.

A person’s public self-image. Positive face is the wish to be liked and approved of; negative face is the wish not to be imposed upon. Requests, criticisms and disagreement threaten face (Brown and Levinson 1987).
Using language to soften a claim or show caution, such as may, seems, perhaps or it could be argued. It is important in academic writing and in polite disagreement.
An utterance whose intended function differs from its grammatical form, such as ‘Can you open the window?’, which is a request rather than a question about ability (Searle 1975).
Softening a statement or request to reduce its force or protect the relationship, for example with I think, perhaps or Could you possibly….
A linguistic means of reducing threat to the listener’s face, such as indirect requests or hedges, as described by Brown and Levinson (1987).

The inability to understand or convey intended meaning because language, though grammatically correct, is inappropriate to the context or relationship, such as an overly direct request to a senior officer (Thomas 1983).

An utterance considered as an action, such as requesting, apologizing, promising or complaining (Austin 1962; Searle 1969). The same act can be performed in more or less direct ways, and appropriateness varies across cultures.
